World.title: Kyle Sandilands repeatedly bullied colleagues, countersuit alleges
World.content:
Kyle Sandilands and Jackie "O" Henderson are being sued in a counter claim by the media company that broadcast their popular radio show, claiming the breakdown of the hosts' partnership posed a serious threat to its financial survival.

ARN Media's The Kyle and Jackie O Show came to an abrupt end in February, when an on-air dispute led to Henderson refusing to work with her co-host of more than 20 years.

The premature ending of the show — whose stars were set to earn a combined $200 million over 10 years — led to Sandilands and Henderson independently launching Federal Court action against their former employer, ARN Media subsidiary Commonwealth Broadcasting Corporation (CBC).

CBC has fought back ahead of a hearing on Friday, launching a counter claim against the duo seeking damages for breach of contract, losses in profit and advertising revenue, and legal costs.

The company's lawyers claimed the relationship breakdown between the hosts threatened to undermine its profitability, court documents revealed.

Letter from Henderson's lawyers significant to case

A key part of the CBC's defence is a letter it received from Henderson's lawyers about a week after the on-air dispute that ultimately led to the hit show's cancellation.

It stated the CBC was "well aware" of Sandilands's bullying, and that a review of its records would provide examples.

"Our client [Henderson] has other examples and audio (both on air and off air) to support a claim of repeated and constant workplace bullying that she has endured at the hands of Mr Sandilands as well as numerous witnesses to the behaviour within the workplace," it read. "The mere fact that this behaviour is frequent and has been continuing for a prolonged period of time also goes to demonstrate that the Group has not taken the required action to act in compliance with its obligations to provide a safe place of work."

Henderson's lawyers said she was left "psychologically unwell" from the "ongoing bullying", some of which was widely reported by media.

The CBC have referenced a letter sent by Henderson's lawyers detailing bullying allegations. (Instagram: @jackieo_official)

It reportedly stated she "cannot continue to work with Mr Sandilands", and "direct contact with Mr Sandilands is now untenable".

It also said she would continue to honour her contract as a presenter, but her return would not be possible until "a suitable alternate day part is found".

Henderson's lawyers said involving the state's workplace regulator would result in a ruling against the CBC.

"Should a report be made to SafeWork NSW, it is now highly likely that the Group will be found to have breached its duty of care to Ms Henderson by exposing her to Mr Sandilands' bullying conduct over a prolonged period," they said.

Examples of alleged repeated bullying

In court documents, the CBC's lawyers said they would argue Sandilands repeatedly denigrated people he worked with on air, from censors to executives, and provided multiple alleged examples dating back to last year.

One example was from a broadcast dated February 11, 2025.

"Don't go bleeping this shit out or you censors will have no job. "Let me explain one more time the bosses have no control whatsoever over what we do on this show. Zero. None. Jackie and I … it starts and ends with what we want to do. "I put my BLEEEP fellas and ladies. We're contracted to do whatever we want to do. And if you don't like it, too bad. There's no one sneaking around in the background fixing shit, cos there's nothing to fix. "I don't give a shit [about shareholders]. I got my money. End of caring."

CBC lawyers said Sandilands was told to comply with four ARN safe work and code of conduct policies in December 2025.

The pair are being counter-sued by their former employer. (Facebook: Kyle and Jackie O)

He had rejected allegations by ARN Media his behaviour met the threshold of serious misconduct, claiming he was wrongfully sacked and eager to return to work.

"Everyone says things from time to time, especially with people that you're close with and it's unfortunate it worked out that way," he said in late March.

"[Henderson] understands, we've had blow ups before. Her on me, me on her. We just get over it usually.

"I think this has all turned into quite a circus."

The matter remains before the court.

World.title: Three children attacked by dingoes in national park
World.content:
A four-year-old girl and her mother have been attacked by a dingo in Karijini National Park, prompting a warning from parks authorities following several similar incidents in recent days.

The WA Parks and Wildlife Service is urging anyone visiting Dales Campground in Karijini to be on the alert.

In a statement, the service said there had been three dingo attacks in recent days.

Campers are being urged to take care in the area. (Supplied: Parks and Wildlife)

The attack on the four-year-old girl happened on Wednesday, with her mother also injured trying to protect her.

Both were taken to Tom Price Hospital for treatment.

Loading...

About 8am am on Saturday, a six-year-old girl was approached by an aggressive dingo that nipped at her clothing in the same location, however she was not injured.

On Monday evening, a six-year-old boy was bitten on the neck and arm.

He was taken to Tom Price Hospital by his parents for medical treatment.

Rangers have been conducting patrols in the area since the Saturday attack to find and destroy the aggressive dingoes.

The DBCA believes three dingoes were involved in the recent attacks. (ABC: Chris Lewis)

A Parks and Wildlife Service staff member from Perth with experience in dingo management flew to the site today.

Wildlife to be 'humanely destroyed'

Speaking to ABC Radio Perth, Hamish Robertson from the Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA) reminded people at the park to exercise caution.

"If a dingo is encountered, please don't approach the dingo or attempt to lure it closer, don't walk alone in Dales Campground in particular, supervise children at all times, and secure food waste," he said.

How dingo behaviour changed on K'gari How history has shaped how we behave towards dingoes.

"If there is something that happens that is a bit negative, make sure you inform a ranger or someone at the visitor centre ... what may seem like a harmless interaction may be an indicator for something that we may need to know."

Mr Robertston, who is the DBCA's Pilbara Regional Leader of Conservation, said rangers identified three possible dingoes involved in the attacks, and they were "patrolling the area and actively trying to trap the dingoes".

He said because dingoes were pack animals and they learnt from each other, the animals in question would be "humanely destroyed".

Dusk and dawn were considered the most dangerous times for attacks, with dingoes being more aggressive this time of year since it was breeding season, according to Mr Roberston.

He said the injured people had all left hospital.

Dales Campground is located a few hundred metres away from the popular Dales Gorge. (ABC News: Michelle Stanley)

Ahead of more visitors planning to visit the park this long weekend, DBCA were speaking to individual campers at Dales Campground, contacting people with bookings and alerting guests through the parks alert system.

Mr Roberston said dingo attacks were rare, and no other campsites were impacted by the recent incidents.

The campground remains open.

World.title: Documents reveal fresh details about Roberts-Smith’s overseas moving plans
World.content:
Investigators were concerned war veteran Ben Roberts-Smith was attempting to move overseas and possibly to Singapore or Spain when he was arrested at Sydney Airport over war crimes allegations, court documents reveal.

The Victoria Cross recipient's arrest as he arrived in Sydney just over a fortnight ago came four days before he was due to depart Australia on April 11 with a destination of Singapore, with a return booking at the end of June.

His partner, Sarah Matulin, was booked to depart the day after him and also return at the end of June.

The details have been revealed in a trove of material that was before the NSW Local Court for his successful bail last week, but only made public by a judge on Thursday.

Mr Roberts-Smith was arrested at Sydney Airport earlier this month.

Mr Roberts-Smith is facing five counts of the war crime of murder and is yet to enter pleas but has categorically denied the allegations.

A statement by the Office of the Special Investigator's (OSI) senior investigating officer, Stephen McIntyre, was tendered on Friday as prosecutors opposed bail, in part by citing the potential risk of flight.

That statement said the OSI had received information the veteran had told his family he intends to travel overseas for the purpose of relocating to Singapore to reside and to establish a business venture.

Euro payment to Spanish company

In November last year, investigators received information that Mr Roberts-Smith was "seeking advice from a financial advisor whether his company, RS Group, could employ his partner and pay her a wage," according to the statement.

The purpose was so that the employment could be relied on in support of a visa to travel to Spain, the officer said.

"The objective of this arrangement was to have Spanish authorities believe that Mr Roberts-Smith's partner had an ongoing source of employment and income."

According to the documents, Mr Roberts-Smith made a payment of 3,320 euros to a Spanish company for immigration law advice.

The statement also said the veteran had recently vacated rented accommodation in Queensland.

Mr Roberts-Smith and his partner had also been voluntarily fingerprinted in Queensland for the purpose of travelling to the US, the documents say.

The veteran was released on bail last week. (ABC News)

Based on the information, the OSI held "concerns" that the 47-year-old was "attempting to relocate to reside in a jurisdiction outside Australia", the McIntyre statement said.

"The ultimate destination and duration of this relocation is unclear as Roberts-Smith's booked flights and family suggest Singapore, whilst the alternative destinations of Spain or USA, have been identified during OSI inquiries.

" The possibility that Roberts-Smith has intended to disguise his travel plans cannot be excluded. "

The document said his "future willingness to return to Australia to face prosecution cannot be judged".

The Crown's submissions during the bail hearing said that the Crown did not suggest Mr Roberts-Smith was "deliberately attempting to evade prosecution" by taking steps to move to Spain.

But the Crown argued the plan was "pursued actively at a time when the applicant would believe that there would be a referral to the Commonwealth DPP in early 2026", and although he was not obliged to notify authorities, his failure to do so "tempers the weight" to be given to an argument he was willing to cooperate and facilitate the charging process.

The apparent plan also "calls into question" the strength of his ties to Queensland and Australia, the Crown argued.

'We never planned to run away'

In an affidavit, Mr Roberts-Smith said he had known about the allegations in various forms for over eight years.

"I deny these allegations and have always done so," he wrote.

Mr Roberts-Smith said he had travelled overseas on nearly 30 occasions since 2018 and was routinely stopped at immigration posts and asked to wait.

"It appeared clear to me this was occurring because I was being investigated by the AFP/OSI."

Mr Roberts-Smith is facing five counts of the war crime of murder. (AAP: Alan Porritt)

In an affidavit, Ms Matulin said she and the veteran had had "countless discussions" since 2020 about remaining in or returning to Australia if he was ever charged.

"Ben and I have travelled overseas and travelled interstate frequently knowing that in any moment police could arrest Ben in relation to these matters," she wrote.

"We never planned to run away from this and have always intended to face the criminal charges if they presented."

Ms Matulin wrote that several years ago the couple started discussing the possible move overseas to "try to create some normalcy in our lives", which has remained "on pause" waiting for charges.

Family and friends "encouraged us to continue to live our lives," she wrote.

Ben Roberts-Smith court case complex A legal expert says the criminal prosecution of former soldier Ben Roberts-Smith will test Australia's war crimes legal framework in ways never seen before, as the case moves toward a trial.

The defence material on the bail application reveals that the pair had looked at places in East Asia to build a business and in 2023 Mr Roberts-Smith travelled to Thailand to prospect business opportunities.

Ms Matulin said by October last year Mr Roberts-Smith submitted several enquiries for listings online about fitness and wellness businesses for sale in Spain.

She said he explained in those enquiries that, for the right opportunity, they could travel "in the next few months".

She said had no prior warning of Mr Roberts-Smith's arrest and the purpose of their staggered departure flights was to accommodate him potentially getting stopped at the airport again — and her missing a flight.

" If we knew this was going to happen, we would not have tried to travel overseas. "

Mr Roberts-Smith was granted bail on a set of conditions, including restrictions on his use of phones and computers, reporting to police three times each week, and a $250,000 security deposit.

His case is expected to return to court in early June.

World.title: How the new eligibility test for NDIS participants could work
World.content:
Labor's plan to create a new "assessment tool" to determine future National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) eligibility based on functional need could backfire without the right settings, say experts.

Peak bodies representing occupational therapists and psychologists have expressed concerns about the reforms going down a "one-size-fits-all" path, but others in the disability sector are cautiously optimistic the correct design will ensure people will get the level of support they need.

The government this week announced sweeping reforms to the NDIS that would slash its cost and ultimately remove 300,000 people previously forecast to be on the scheme by 2030.

A core component of the proposed reforms involves scrapping a set list of impairments which automatically guaranteed eligibility, to a new assessment tool which considers an individual's functional capacity.

New tool to determine eligibility

Health Minister Mark Butler has said the "objective assessment tool" would be produced with input from a technical advisory group, people with disability and the states and territories.

"That will govern entry to the scheme, in my expectation, from the first of January 2028," he said.

"It will be the tool that governs reassessment of people, which happens at the end of their plans."

Mark Butler says the tool will be designed in consultation with key groups. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The NDIS has previously guaranteed access to people whose diagnosis was featured on a list of severe and permanent impairments, such as autism spectrum disorder or spinal cord injury.

The new system would scrap that "access list" and instead consider what level of support a person required based on their ability to independently manage everyday tasks.

It is understood the government will look to examples like the World Health Organisation (WHO) Disability Assessment Schedule to inform its plan.

In 2012, the WHO suggested a standard instrument for functional assessments that was diagnosis-neutral and could be used across physical, mental, neurological and substance-related conditions.

Disability community surprised by scale of planned NDIS cuts NDIS Minister Mark Butler has defended the government's latest cost-cutting changes to the scheme in an interview with the ABC, amid an avalanche of participant concern.

It measures difficulty over six domains, including cognition, mobility, self-care, "getting along" in social interactions and relationship and life activities like household responsibilities, work or study.

Under the WHO model, respondents rate the degree of difficulty on a five-point scale from "none" through to "cannot do" for each area.

People answer based on how they usually perform activities, including the use of aids or personal assistance, and refer to the past 30 days to get an average of good and bad days.

'Right' functional assessment could help children with autism

Professor Nicole Rinehart, who is the director of the neurodevelopment program at Monash University's school of psychological sciences, said the "right" functional assessment system would ensure children with autism got the support they needed.

"Autism has a very uneven profile," she said.

"If you had two children with autism and they both have an IQ of 100, that's not going to tell you anything about their functional needs because of the sheer complexity of it, things like neurological impairments or motor functioning."

Nicole Rinehart urged against adopting a "blunt" assessment tool for children with autism. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Professor Rinehart, who is also the founder of the AllPlay program for children living with disabilities, said the government must be "really careful" not to deploy a "blunt instrument" of assessment.

"Get the right people around the table and look at each child as an individual child," she said.

"This is a human exercise. This isn't some levelling exercise, it's complex."

Professor Rinehart said the new assessment system must retain "open doors" between programs like Thriving Kids and the NDIS so that if a child needed to move from one to the other, it was possible.

"If an autistic child is on one developmental trajectory and they start showing regression, they need to start as quickly as possible on the NDIS to get the intensive support that will help them developmentally," she said.

Assessment tool 'insulting' to allied health professionals

Michelle Oliver, chief occupational therapist at Occupational Therapists Australia, said performing functional capacity assessments was "core business" for the sector, and questioned the accuracy of a government tool operating as a catch-all test for NDIS eligibility.

"I think we would be insulted if functional capacity assessments were taken out of our space and put into an administrative role," she said.

Michelle Oliver says occupational therapists undergo years of training to assess people with disability. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Ms Oliver said occupational therapists applied a range of tools to accurately assess people's needs, from adults with schizophrenia to children with cerebral palsy.

"That's quite insulting for an OT — who has a university degree and worked for many years to develop those skills — to then just think you can pull a tool and get an administrative role to execute that," she said.

Amanda Curran, chief psychologist at the Australian Association of Psychologists, agreed one tool was "never going to capture every need that a person has".

"That's why they go to specialists like psychologists and OTs, because we're trained in assessment," she said.

"We know which assessments to pick and put together to help reflect the accurate picture of that person."

Disability advocates cautiously support focus on functional capacity

Disability Advocacy Network Australia chief executive Emma Bennison said assessing functional capacity to establish access to the NDIS "makes very good sense".

"I think getting into the question of diagnosis and levels of diagnosis … is fraught with subjectivity and complexity," she said.

But Ms Bennison said any assessment tool must be developed in consultation with people with disability, and said there were still a lot of questions about how it would work.

She also said she did not want anyone removed from the NDIS without guaranteed access to alternative support, particularly those with complex psychosocial disabilities.

"Otherwise we'll have people going off the scheme into an abyss," she said.

"We will probably see people taking their own lives if they're forced off of the scheme without there being adequate supports to act as a safety net for them."

World.title: AFL LIVE: Blakey could face scrutiny for late hit as Dogs, Swans trade goals in blockbuster clash
World.content:
St Kilda’s Lance Collard has had his penalty for using a homophobic slur in a VFL game reduced to four weeks (with two weeks suspended until the end of 2027) by the AFL Appeals Board, which described the original penalty as “crippling” for the player.

The appeals board, led by Will Houghton KC, backed the AFL Disciplinary Tribunal’s decision to find Collard guilty but said their decision to ban him for seven weeks (and two suspended) was “manifestly excessive”.

Lance Collard has been hit with a four-week ban. AFL Photos

It is the second time in two years Collard has been found to have used homophobic language in a match, however he denied using the phrase “f---ing f----t” in this match against Frankston.

After admitting to using the slur in a VFL match in 2024, he was suspended for six matches. On this occasion, Collard said he used the word maggot, however two Frankston players said he had used the homophobic slur. The AFL Disciplinary Tribunal found him guilty of using the slur and the appeals board said they were open to make that finding and there had been no error of law.

Plans have emerged for a new “mid-market” apartment tower draped with greenery in the middle of Brisbane. A development application for the 15-storey building at 39 Lambert Street in Kangaroo Point was lodged with Brisbane City Council. It would have 52 units, a pool, gym, spa, yoga lawn and lounge and dining areas. An artist impression of planned tower at 39 Lambert Street in Kangaroo Point, Brisbane. Keylin All but four apartments would have two bedrooms.



No detail about the premium units have been provided, other than that they would be “sky homes” with uninterrupted views. Artist impressions show extensive greenery draped over the building and hanging from balconies. Three levels of underground parking and bike storage would also be built. The 1012-square-metre site has been an empty block since about 2018. It was previously occupied by a two-storey, white-brick apartment building.



Keylin is behind the development, with Jackson Teece doing the architecture work. CoStruct is the planned builder. The building at 39 Lambert Street in Kangaroo Point would include a pool, gym, spa, yoga lawn, and lounge and dining areas. Keylin “The area offers an enviable blend of outdoor recreation and urban energy ... riverside walkways, lush parks, and a thriving selection of restaurants, cafes and bars,” Keylin managing director Louis Cheung said in a statement. “There has been a noticeable gap in the delivery of well-designed, mid-market apartments in this suburb.” Related Article Brisbane development Property bloom: Construction set to begin on West End tower at site of former florist



Apartment development in Brisbane has been concentrated heavily in the top of the market over the past 12 months, with many primarily comprising units with three-bedrooms or more. World.title: Discount fuel and cash giveaways: How Adrian Portelli’s business works
World.content:
NationalPetrol prices Discount fuel and cash giveaways: How Adrian Portelli’s business works Stephen Brook April 23, 2026 — 7:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Businessman Adrian Portelli was back in the news on Thursday after opening his new venture, selling fuel for $1 a litre at a petrol station in Preston. Also back in the news: questions about how the entrepreneur’s LMCT+ membership-based shopping discount and giveaway business actually works, and whether it is an unlicensed lottery, as critics and a South Australian regulator assert. Entrepreneur Adrian Portelli selling cheap fuel to his LMCT+ members at his petrol station in Preston today. Paul Jeffers On Thursday, the Preston petrol station was not ensnarled in the kind of traffic chaos that was seen at an earlier unrelated fuel giveaway in Truganina, organised by RS Rewards on Good Friday, which was shut down by police. But the cheap fuel is only available to members of LCMT+, who pay a monthly subscription fee to access hundreds of thousands of dollars’ worth of discounts, as well as cash and prize giveaways.



The new fuel membership will cost $99.99 a year, which gives members access to petrol at the wholesale price, Portelli told this masthead, adding that he launched the business after petrol companies declined to join his scheme. The Preston petrol station venture was not making money, he said. “We are not depending on this venture to turn a profit, it is a soft launch to test our [petrol station] employees,” he said. Over time, the number of petrol sites will expand. “We can’t lose money; otherwise, we will run out of money. ” LMCT+ is billed as a subscription platform that offers discounts to more than 2000 businesses. These include Ultratune, Elite Supplements, Rip Curl, home appliance shop Betta, Adore Beauty Interior Secrets and Frank & Beans Underwear. The business makes its money from subscriptions, as well as ticket sales for individual giveaways.



Until recently, there were three tiers of LMCT+ memberships. An entry-level membership, which goes for $19.99 a month, allows members to claim up to $50,000 in savings from affiliate businesses each year. With a premium membership ($49.99 a month), the annual savings cap increases to $150,000, and for the elite membership ($99.99 a month), it’s up to $250,000. The fuel membership, which costs $99.99 annually, will be available soon. Related Article Exclusive

Gambling Billionaire Adrian Portelli wants to sell you petrol as UK move raises gambling concerns Memberships also include a limited number of entries into LMCT’s famed giveaways, which became popularised thanks to Portelli’s appearances and purchases on The Block. On Thursday on ABC Radio, during an expletive-laden interview, Portelli denied he was cashing in on the fuel crisis or that his business was a gambling operation. “How is that gambling? We are using a trade promotion to promote the app,” Portelli, whose wealth has been estimated at $1.6 billion, told ABC Radio Melbourne.



Later that day he told this masthead: “When someone is choosing not to understand … That is the response you are going to get from me.” LMCT+, which stands for Licensed Motor Car Trader Plus, was founded by Portelli in 2018. The businessman became famous for buying up properties on home renovation program The Block, broadcast on Channel Nine (Nine owns this masthead), and offering them as giveaways on LMCT+. The program dubbed him “Lambo Guy” after a fondness for Lamborghini cars. Winner Brad (who requested a pseudonym as he didn’t want to be identified) received a winning call from Portelli telling him he had won either a house featured on The Block or $2.5 million. Related Article Petrol prices Free fuel hero or regulatory rebel? The chequered past of the man behind the Good Friday gridlock Brad, a business manager, was never an LMCT+ member but spent about $1200 over the previous year buying tickets for specific draws, also entitling him to shopping discounts, which he never used.



“If the person who won is not a member, they [members] tend to crack the shits,” said Brad, who added that he had missed watching the live draw on Facebook. “I was going to watch it and got into a conservation with my wife about something and my phone started ringing. I then jumped online and saw my name. “I didn’t believe it. In that moment, you are in shock.” Portelli called personally to announce the prize but at first “played coy” at the start by telling him he hadn’t won the lesser prizes before revealing he had the choice of $2.5 million or a house. Brad, who met Portelli by chance after his win, said he felt the businessman was the victim of the tall poppy syndrome. “You see the genuine excitement he gets; that’s what I take away from it.



“But I am going to have a different opinion to someone who hasn’t won,” he added, declining to reveal which prize he accepted. In South Australia, LMCT+ and Portelli are appealing against a ruling that found parent company Xclusive Tech Pty Ltd was guilty of conducting unlawful lotteries and fined it $40,000. Portelli was acquitted on personal charges and has threatened defamation action against the former South Australian gambling minister over her comments. “We run a legitimate business,” Portelli said. LMCT+ is running what it dubs the “the biggest giveaway in Australian television history” alongside Channel Seven and its new program My Reno Rules, after Portelli bought two homes in the Melbourne suburb of Bulleen that he intends to give away to the public on June 2.



The site has a live countdown to the giveaway draw, and any Australian resident over 18 can buy individual tickets to the prize draw, without subscribing. In the My Reno Rules giveaway, which promises winners the choice between one of the two houses or $2 million in cash, tickets go for as little as $10 for three entries, all the way up to $500 (1500 entries). The business says it is “fully licensed under Trade Promotion Lottery laws”, but gambling reform advocates are critical, saying the business operates through legal loopholes. Tim Costello, chief advocate for the Alliance for Gambling Reform, is a critic of Portelli and the gambling regulation system. “I think he has driven his Lamborghini through the loophole in gambling regulation,” Costello said. Costello said Australia operated in a “Swiss cheese patchwork of regulation” and national regulation was needed. He was also critical of the cheap petrol initiative.



“This is very clever. He will be seen by the public as the people’s hero. This is why he is a billionaire.” Earlier this month, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced a crackdown on “harmful and emerging online lottery products”, but did not name any specific businesses. “What is everywhere is innovative gambling,” Costello said. “You have prediction markets where you can bet on the Strait of Hormuz opening or closing. “There are so many offshore companies that are beyond any regulation. The online betting market is growing at 50 per cent a year.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Rinehart to hand over financial records to court rivals
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMining Rinehart to hand over financial records to court rivals Michael Philipps April 23, 2026 — 7:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

The decades-long legal battle that saw the descendants of iron ore pioneer Peter Wright claim victory against Gina Rinehart’s Hancock Prospecting will soon land in the hands of its fourth judge, as a row over the calculation of royalties brews. Rinehart is likely to be forced to hand over years of financial records to two rival mining dynasties. The WA Supreme Court judge who handed down the ruling in the case may not be available to oversee the ultimate decision of the royalties involved. Last week Justice Jennifer Smith ruled that Wright Prospecting was entitled to half of the historical royalties from the Hope Downs mines, estimated to be worth hundreds of millions of dollars. However, last year Smith was re-appointed as an Auxiliary Judge of the Supreme Court of Western Australia with her 12-month term beginning on June 5, 2025.



At the follow-up hearing to decide how the costs involved in the landmark case would be divided on Thursday, Smith said there will need to be some changes to the orders that the parties involved have proposed. “Having heard the parties this morning, there is a sufficient issue that has been raised that there are particulars of law that may not be able to be managed by a judge and should be handled by a referee,” she said. “Ultimately, both of these matters are appropriate to be defined by a referee and not an officer of a court “As I won’t be here much longer as a member of this court, I feel it is most appropriate that another judge make that decision.” Rinehart is likely to be forced to hand over years of financial records to two rival mining dynasties pursuing hundreds of millions of dollars in unpaid iron ore royalties.



Lawyers for Rinehart’s company, Hancock Prospecting, and the heirs of mining pioneer Peter Wright and engineer Don Rhodes wrangled over the implementation of a judgment that found Wright Prospecting and DFD Rhodes were owed some of the spoils from the massive Rio Tinto-operated Hope Downs mining complex, in WA’s ore-rich Pilbara region. These included who should calculate the royalty amounts, the interest rates that could be applied to the vast sum, potential damages for Hancock Prospecting’s breach of contract, future revenue payments and what documents Hancock Prospecting would be required to supply. In setting out her judgment last week, Smith called the decision only a “half-win” as she rejected Wright Prospecting’s claim for part ownership of another portion of the mining project, allowing Rinehart to keep her status as the country’s wealthiest person with an estimated fortune of $38 billion. Wright’s heirs, which include billionaire Angela Bennett and her nieces, Leonie Baldock and Alexandra Burt, argued that their family company was entitled to a 1.25 per cent royalty from the Hope Downs iron ore mines in WA’s Pilbara region. Hancock Prospecting runs the lucrative mines with mining giant Rio Tinto.



The tenements were first pegged by Hancock and Wright in the 1940s, and in 1982, the iron ore pioneers nutted out an agreement to divide the assets that was intended to prevent their descendants from arguing over ownership in the future. The parties will return to court on May 1 to continue the hearing. With AAP

World.title: Heard Geese, the ‘saviours of rock’n’roll’? That might not be an accident
World.content:
CultureMusicSocial media Opinion Heard Geese, the ‘saviours of rock’n’roll’? That might not be an accident Benjamin Potter Journalist April 23, 2026 — 7:30pm

April 23, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

As someone who listens to music religiously, I try to block out a lot of the online hype whenever I come across a new artist. Take American singer-songwriter Mk.gee, for example. “The modern-day Prince” got bandied around online so heavily after the 2024 release of his debut album, Two Star & The Dream Police, that it immediately sent me running for the hills. I only came around once a friend told me almost a year later that I should listen. It’s now probably one of my favourite records of the past five years, but it was the lost art of “word-of-mouth” that encouraged me to take the plunge. Geese perform at Laneway Festival in Melbourne in February. Rick Clifford There’s something to be said for the simple act of discovering music organically because, let’s face it, we’re saturated. We’re forever attuned to what’s on our algorithm rather than crate-digging at our local record store to find an album that beckons with its well-considered cover art. The upside of this though is that more quirky, “hard-to-market” music has now been able to cut through and be successful. In a bygone era, bands that regularly had mainstream appeal like Ween and Primus were considered to have cult followings that the labels wouldn’t bother touching. By no means were their fan bases considered small, but they were niche and weren’t the types to also pick up a Boyz II Men record.



Streaming and social media algorithms have not only changed the way we consume music, they’ve also changed the way our musical psyches work. But the reception for the fourth album from New York-based Geese, Getting Killed, an album characterised by its brash, tumultuous songwriting, has illustrated the use of morally dubious industry practices. I didn’t care much for this record when it came out, and I still don’t. Musically, there are plenty of interesting things about it, but what was most peculiar to me at the time was for how unconventional it was, the reception seemed disproportionate – so manufactured in its consent that it would have made Noam Chomsky raise an eyebrow. How did a relatively experimental band gain enough online traction to become what The Guardian has labelled “the saviours of rock’n’roll” in less than a year? Last month, the co-founders of popular US digital marketing agency Chaotic Good, Jesse Coren and Andrew Spelman, joined a Billboard panel at South by Southwest (SXSW) to discuss how songs go viral in 2026 and openly admitted to manipulating online discourse for artists as a social media marketing tactic. “All opinions are formed in the TikTok comments, which is a reminder to us of what we can help with,” Coren said. “I don’t know if this will make anyone feel better, but a lot of what we do on the narrative side is controlling the discourse. Most people see a video … and that first comment they see becomes their opinion, even when they haven’t heard the whole album. It’s really important for us to make sure we’re ahead of it and controlling that narrative in the direction we want.”



Related Article New music He’s been called Gen Z’s Bob Dylan and praised by Nick Cave. But is Cameron Winter for real? In essence, what Chaotic Good manufactures for its clients is a “grassroots” movement. According to Wired magazine, it commands an army of fake social media accounts to flood the algorithm with an artist’s music, hiding tracks in the background of videos and staging “organic” interactions in comment sections through those same accounts to increase engagement. Spelman calls it “trend simulation” – fandom designed to trigger the TikTok and YouTube algorithms. By the time a real listener discovers the artist, the “conversation” they’re joining is often nothing more than a well-funded marketing mirage. Shortly after the Billboard panel, US musician and writer Eliza McLamb linked Geese’s online success directly to Chaotic Good’s client roster, where they were reportedly touted as a prime example of successful “narrative control”. Wired labelled the fanfare around the band a “psyop”(a planned use of communication or propaganda to influence behaviour). Chaotic Good has since removed these references from its website, but the connection remains a focal point for those wondering how much of the band’s “grassroots” acclaim was truly spontaneous and how much was a carefully executed plan. New York-based band Geese has been thrust into controversy with their connection to marketing agency Chaotic Good. OK McCausland/The New York Times



While this may feel existential to some, today, these practices are not unusual in the music industry. Some may argue that it’s not that different to how it used to be. Putting up posters, standing on the street begging people to listen to your demo; it’s always been about creating your own hype, but to what end is at best questionable and at worst morally offensive because it treats the listener as a target to be manipulated, not someone to be connected with. There’s no doubt Geese have earned their stripes and for people who genuinely love their music, it wasn’t just sly marketing that pushed them to become fans. You don’t become successful without your music being good, but practices employed by agencies such as Chaotic Good exemplify a growing class divide within the industry. It creates a “pay-to-play” landscape where the barrier to entry isn’t defined by just talent, but the capital required to manufacture the very “word-of-mouth” that used to be free. For the real Geese fans, please don’t put a bomb in my car. Benjamin Potter is the SEO editor of The Sydney Morning Herald. He is also a music writer and a local music producer. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Lack of chargers stalls grand plans for electric cars
World.content:
EnvironmentClimate changeElectric vehicles Lack of chargers stalls grand plans for electric cars Nick O'Malley April 23, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

As electric vehicle uptake surges, Australia’s charging network is failing to keep up with growing demand, leaving drivers queuing at charging stations and the industry demanding governments clear “lumbering monopolies” in the energy sector. In Australia, there are 45 electric cars for every charging point compared with a global average of 11, according to the International Energy Agency. Some in the industry claim the rollout is being slowed down by the electricity network providers, which own the grid’s poles and wires, and which are seeking to expand into the charging market. As a record number of drivers buy EVs, sales figures for petrol and diesel vehicles are declining. Louie Douvis “Industry stands ready to support Australians who urgently want more electric vehicle charging infrastructure as part of the EV boom,” said David McElrea, the Smart Energy Council’s acting chief executive. “However, it can take up to two years and $350,000 for networks to connect new chargers to the grid.” His comments were echoed by a Tesla spokesperson, who said the rollout of kerbside chargers was being slowed by high fees and long connection ties imposed by the network owners.



Sean McGinty, whose company EVX builds and operates kerbside chargers, said the network monopolies control 90 per cent of the costs to the EV charging market, and there was “good reason” that they were not allowed to own charging infrastructure in competition. Related Article Electric vehicles How to get mass adoption of EVs in city areas? It’s not just about public chargers “The spectre of monopoly DNSPs [distribution network service providers] entering the competitive EV charging market is slowing investment in EV infrastructure. Perversely, they are creating the problem they’re spruiking to be saviour of.” EVX is one of a dozen companies and industry organisations to sign a joint statement calling for Australian governments to establish clear rules preventing energy networks from entering the charging sector and requiring them to improve connection times and provide clear fee structures. “We stand ready to invest, build and operate the public charging infrastructure Australia needs to support the shift away from volatile imported fuels and toward locally powered transport,” says that statement, whose signatories include the Australian Energy Council, the Smart Energy Council as well as Tesla and AGL.



”Under the right policy settings, the private sector is ready to deploy billions of dollars of cumulative investment by 2030 to expand Australia’s charging network at speed and scale. Australia now needs a clearly defined partnership between government, regulators, networks and industry.“ Stephanie Bashir, chief executive of the industry consultancy Nexa Advisory, said the sector had the capacity to rapidly expand Australia’s network of chargers if governments provided certainty. “Bottom line – private sector investment will come if competition is enabled and protected. Innovation at speed and scale is not a place for lumbering monopolies or political interference and vested interests.” Energy Networks Australia, whose members include giants such as Ausgrid, Essential Energy and Transgrid, agrees EV charger deployment is lagging in Australia, but argues that it would be accelerated if its members were allowed to fully enter the market. It has submitted a rule change request to the Australian Energy Market Commission (AEMC) to help accelerate the process, while in NSW the networks are lobbying the Minns government to scrap rules preventing them from expanding into EV charging. Emma Shanks, chief external affairs officer for Energy Networks Australia, said the networks were not seeking to enter the fast-charging market, but were focused on pole-mounted chargers commonly seen in urban areas, which ENA believes should be treated like any other electricity infrastructure. Shanks said its members wanted to be allowed to install and maintain the chargers, but not to act as retailers selling electricity from them.



She said the high costs and wait times referred to in the public statement probably referred to larger fast-charging stations, which in some cases needed as much power as a 12-storey apartment building and required upgrades to grid infrastructure. Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen said the government was looking closely at the charging network. “Australia’s EV charging network increased by 20 per cent in 2025 – it’s clear that the private sector is entering this market as more and more Australians take up cheaper to run, cleaner cars,” Bowen said. “There remains work to do in the more remote and regional areas – this is some of the most challenging areas and the government sees it as an important public service.” The war in Iran has prompted a surge in demand for EVs in Australia. One in seven cars sold in March was electric, while EV sales around the world leapt by 20 per cent last year, with around 21 million cars sold.



Over Easter, the popularity of the vehicles left many drivers in queues for charging stations on the road between Sydney and Melbourne. Dr Stephen Lightfoot, a vice president of the Australian Conservation Foundation, said he had been “feeling pretty smug” about driving between NSW and Victoria over the long weekend, knowing he would save money by avoiding fuel costs in his EV. But the drive was complicated by long waits for chargers along the highway from Sydney to Melbourne, exacerbated by faulty charging equipment and the need to download different phone apps to access power at different charge sites. The difficulty in accessing chargers added to range anxiety and slowed electrification of the fleet despite the savings offered by EVs, he said. “Emissions for light vehicles is 10 per cent of our total emissions and we have to get that down. At present, queues like the ones we saw at Easter are playing on people’s minds.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.content:
NationalQueenslandBrisbane development New ‘mid-market’ inner-city apartment tower plans revealed William Davis April 23, 2026 — 8:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Plans have emerged for a new “mid-market” apartment tower draped with greenery in the middle of Brisbane. A development application for the 15-storey building at 39 Lambert Street in Kangaroo Point was lodged with Brisbane City Council. It would have 52 units, a pool, gym, spa, yoga lawn and lounge and dining areas. An artist impression of planned tower at 39 Lambert Street in Kangaroo Point, Brisbane. Keylin All but four apartments would have two bedrooms.



No detail about the premium units have been provided, other than that they would be “sky homes” with uninterrupted views. Artist impressions show extensive greenery draped over the building and hanging from balconies. Three levels of underground parking and bike storage would also be built. The 1012-square-metre site has been an empty block since about 2018. It was previously occupied by a two-storey, white-brick apartment building.



Keylin is behind the development, with Jackson Teece doing the architecture work. CoStruct is the planned builder. The building at 39 Lambert Street in Kangaroo Point would include a pool, gym, spa, yoga lawn, and lounge and dining areas. Keylin “The area offers an enviable blend of outdoor recreation and urban energy ... riverside walkways, lush parks, and a thriving selection of restaurants, cafes and bars,” Keylin managing director Louis Cheung said in a statement. “There has been a noticeable gap in the delivery of well-designed, mid-market apartments in this suburb.” Related Article Brisbane development Property bloom: Construction set to begin on West End tower at site of former florist



Apartment development in Brisbane has been concentrated heavily in the top of the market over the past 12 months, with many primarily comprising units with three-bedrooms or more. The development application had not been uploaded to the council website on Thursday evening. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: On NDIS, changes will hopefully resolve failings
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters On NDIS, changes will hopefully resolve failings April 23, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

See no evil. Cathy Wilcox To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. We welcome the government overhauling the NDIS. Two members of my family have been participants since its inception and the scheme has been essential. However, it has fostered a culture of reliance as opposed to one of independence. We observe this at the individual level with participants allocated support workers who have no notion of the practice of support work. There is no discourse around the models of learning and support, the social model of disability, discriminatory practice and the right to be purposefully engaged with one’s community. The workers, sent by a registered provider, will have little or no information about the person’s goals.

Local councils and the state government have largely withdrawn support for community building, services, employment opportunities, creative pursuits, education support and inclusion. Perhaps this is more starkly felt in Victoria. The NDIS has funded individuals that too often find themselves in segregated, expensive, poorly operated, registered programs with no pathways out. Currently anyone can be a registered provider, just pay the costs. All documents can be bought to present for audit. To change this will be a huge undertaking from the whole community.

Jenny Harrison, Footscray Unintended consequences of rejig

Registration of providers in the NDIS scheme to assist those with disabilities is designed, with good reason, to weed out shonky providers who rort the system. However, unfortunately, an unintended consequence is that the costs of mandatory registration will inhibit very small business, sole trader providers (currently unregistered) from continuing to take part in the scheme because they help a limited numbers of clients, whom they see only once a week, with a range of disabilities, but possibly only one or two who are on the NDIS.

The start-up registration of $3000-$10,000, plus ongoing fees, far outweighs the income from these few NDIS clients. It will mean that parents will be unable to use NDIS support to pay for some services they need for their children, specialist services provided by highly qualified and experienced, very small, sole trader providers. It would be hoped that, in the rejig of NDIS, a solution to this problem is found.

Janet Roberts, Director of Learning Pathways, Templestowe Lower The participants are not the problem

The Albanese government says its latest NDIS reforms are about “saving” the scheme for future generations. Fine. But stop pretending participants are the problem. I am an NDIS participant. My personalised wheelchair cost $27,000 and my ankle support cost $7000, both funded by the scheme. I was then provided with a more comfortable support costing just $200.

That does not point to participants recklessly wasting public money. It points to a system that too often makes poor decisions, while people with disability are left to live with the consequences. I also had to beg for an instruction manual for $10,000 worth of assistive technology – and I never received it. That is not luxury. That is basic accountability failing. If the government genuinely wants to protect the NDIS, it should focus on inflated pricing, fraudsters and bad providers, not feed the lazy narrative that disabled people are to blame for the blowout.

Participants did not create this mess. We should not be punished for it. Disabled Australians are not responsible for the rorting. We are the reason the NDIS exists.

Name and address supplied



Rethink on government priorities is a priority

Interesting how we can’t afford to keep the mildly disabled on the NDIS but can still afford submarines, fossil fuel subsidies, private school funding, negative gearing, capital gains tax concessions, the private health insurance rebate, franking credit cash refunds, and the stage-three tax cuts.

Fabio Scalia, Balaclava THE FORUM A disgruntled senior

If I sound disgruntled then, believe me, I am. The federal government has decided to “disincentivise” private health insurance for aged pensioners. Could be it’s a push to make us rely on the public health system. My God, let it not be so.

I am 87 years old. I maintain private health insurance because I have health issues; they are serious enough to need semi-urgent (but not necessarily emergency) surgery but I have had four surgery procedures over the past 15 months, not because they were emergency but to prevent them becoming that.

If I was relying on the public system where it takes up to two years to talk to a specialist and be diagnosed, candidly, I’d be dead now.

I receive a part pension. It costs me a quarter of that pension each month to cover the private health insurance premiums. Removal of the seniors rebate means I will pay more to stay alive. It can only be that the government is gouging elderly citizens.

I have every right to be disgruntled.

Noel Mavric, Moonlight Flat Keep being bold . . .

The federal government has made a courageous decision to make much needed changes to the NDIS in light of the unsustainability and poor implementation and outrageous exploitation of this life-changing social program. With this overhaul, Health Minister Mark Butler has flagged a change to aspects of social and community supports that clearly warrant a rethink. However, for people with lifelong disability being part of and included in their community has, and always will be, a fundamental aspiration. The proposed Inclusive Communities Fund is intended to address this important aspect, let’s hope it doesn’t fall short.

We now await further bold and courageous decisions by the government as it finalises the budget.

Tax reform must be a headline item to not only address intergenerational inequity but provide the means to fund programs that improve the life of our most vulnerable citizens.

Anne Lyon, Camberwell . . . And brave

Now is the time for the Albanese government to implement the bold reforms that the economy needs. We cannot go on giving away our natural resources and adding to a foreign debt that is going to hit $1trillion this year. If it’s necessary to control spending or reduce tax incentives, so be it.

The world is in a precarious position, and it will probably be for the foreseeable future with more disruptors such as AI coming online. Some sacrifices will be necessary, and we’ll surely hear the screams of those affected, but we shouldn’t miss the golden opportunity that this budget offers to set things right.

This government was elected with an overwhelming majority, so let’s be brave and implement the policies that Australians are calling for.

George Fernandez, Eltham North



Different approach

I am not a doctor but I can still generate a prescription: AUKUS out. A softer and more humane reform of NDIS in.

David Rose, Nollamara, WA True Australian values

Discussion about Australian values is humbug. What are these values? The people in my family or friendship networks who are migrants arrived here with very little. Through persistence and hard work they have achieved what most would consider a comfortable life for their families. They have contributed emotionally, physically and financially to Australia’s success. They will tell you that Australia is the greatest place on Earth and they are lucky to be here. I would think that these are Australian values. They are not the enemy. Let’s call out this discussion for what it is, dog whistling racism.

Australia can and should do better than the current trajectory. We cannot afford to let the likes of One Nation and the United Australia Party hoodwink us with empty slogans that demonise people to satisfy their political expediency.

Steve Griffin, West Coburg Players under spotlight

AFL matches are analysed within an inch of their lives by the footy pundits in media. While the footballers are well remunerated, many are often virtually humiliated by what they did or didn’t do by the experts, many of whom are former players (granted some are worse at doing this than others).

Nevertheless, I shudder to think what the mental health would be like for employees in other workplaces if they were publicly shamed on a regular basis like AFL footballers are.

Phil Alexander, Eltham An F for figurative

It should not be surprising or a secret that the stellar performers on the NAPLAN writing test use figurative language more and more confidently than less competent writers (“There’s a secret to scoring top marks in NAPLAN Writing. And it’s easily missed by students”, 21/4). The suggestion that some figurative language criteria should be added to 10 current NAPLAN criteria for assessment is ill-judged.

The test has too many specific criteria that distort markers’ views of the level of development and quality of performance of students on that test. It is widely accepted among writer assessment specialists that the NAPLAN criteria are reductive.

The writing of students has been damaged by this regressive writing test that the 2020 McGaw review of NAPLAN recommended should be discontinued until it can be replaced with a better test.

The Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority could not recognise that the test it had designed and used for more than 10 years was deficient, and no change was made.

The writing test would not be improved by adding figurative language to the current crowd of 10 criteria, and teachers should not be wasting time teaching students about figurative language in the hope of improving their writing. With more than 30 per cent not reaching the expected standard in year 9, students should not be distracted with issues like figurative language when so many are struggling to communicate clearly and coherently.

Doug McCurry, Eaglemont Where’s the details?

Pauline Hanson is accused of offering simplistic solutions to complex problems (″⁣One Nation tyre kickers, careful you don’t buy a lemon″⁣, 23/4). One Nation has policies, but few details, including on immigration, cost of living, renewable energy and law-and-order. Their overall ethos is of individual freedom, and minimum government intervention.

It’s not just One Nation voters who fail to study full policy detail from various parties and candidates. For example, in the Nepean state electorate, the public/private funding and administration options for a new hospital at Rosebud are complex.

Many people will be kicking thetyres of One Nation, at byelections in Nepean (state) and Farrer (federal), plus the Victorian state elections.

Labor and the LNP must sell their policies, with enough believable detail to edge ahead of attractive One Nation slogans.

John Hughes, Mentone



Tax gas giants

Of course energy security is front of mind for the government (“Push for more tax on gas hit by a world of trouble”, 22/4). But cost-of-living pressures and climate change should be factors, too. LNG companies operating in Australia have made $112 billion in profits since 2022 and Australians have seen very little of that revenue. The funds raised from properly taxing these corporations could support Australians in myriad ways.

Larni Dibben, Glen Iris Dud and dumper

History will record its own nicknames for Donald Trump (Letters, 23/4), but for my money he’s Donald the Dud. Like a leaky balloon, his grandiose threats promise the world but wither away to nothing. Or perhaps Donald the Dump: the first US President to be dismissed from office?

Jenifer Nicholls, Windsor Worthless threats

Donald Trump reminds me of the irresponsible parent who tries to discipline his young kids by threatening them with impossible punishments. As soon as they understand that such punishments are not forthcoming, all parental threats and control are lost.

Les Aisen, Elsternwick Undue influence

Please, can we ban the ″⁣influencers″⁣ who seem to be increasingly infiltrating our lives, even on the hallowed pages of The Age. I am not interested in these self-absorbed and self-promoting Ken and Barbie doll people with their shiny plastic faces, perfect pouts and perfect pecs. I am not interested in their perfect lives, their perfect children, their enormous houses, what they had for breakfast or where they go for holidays. Could The Age, at least, be an influencer free zone?

April Baragwanath, Geelong We’re being played

That’s what it’s all about isn’t it (″⁣US Navy declares Australia ready to start hosting nuclear subs″⁣ 22/4)? Perth becomes a defacto US naval base while they dangle the lure of a nuclear sub in 20 years maybe, and charge us billions every year for the privilege of being hoodwinked. Is there any limit to our national stupidity?

John Laurie, Riddells Creek



Nice day for a wedding

Your correspondent (Letters, 23/4) asks does anyone remember such warm April weather? Sixty-four years plus two days ago my wife and I were married on Easter Saturday April 21, 1962, on an 84F (now 29C) degree day.

The weather had been warm all that week and continued, only turning cold in early May.

Thomas Hogg, East Melbourne Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Trump

Did Donald Trump really expect Iran to open the Strait of Hormuz while he blocked all Iranian ports?

Corrado Tavella, Rosslyn Park, SA Hasn’t Donald Trump heard about the boy who cried wolf?

Campbell Paine, Toorak



If it’s “OK″⁣ for the US to instigate regime change, does that mean it would be OK, in theory, for another country to address the increasing need for regime change in the US?

Claire Merry, Wantirna If we didn’t know before let’s hope we do now. The first casualty of war is truth. Bluffing, empty threats are a big part of the artillery on both sides.

Gordon Thurlow, Mooloolah Valley, Qld Re your correspondent’s suggested labels for Donald Trump (Letters, 23/4), for years I’ve referred to him as Agent Orange.

Barbara Hilling, Watsonia Nth In years to come Trump the Terrible may be an appropriate name for a president who will go down in history for being just that.

Ruth Davis, Carrum Furthermore

Japan has fascinated me for many years but Alex Reszelska’s Comment (23/4), turned fascination to wonder and yearning.

Betty Rudin,Wandin North



Your correspondent (Letters, 23/4) says AI should stand for Assisted Intelligence. Dairy cattle breeders have been working successfully with AI for at least 60years – Artificial Insemination.

Alan McLean, Queenscliff I place my trust in Actual Intelligence.

David Johnston, Healesville With the government getting tough on the NDIS and seniors’ health insurance, I wait to see how tough it gets with the gas industry.

Pauline Ashton, Maribyrnong Finally

I’m waiting for the announcement that we will all be given free cake for the rest of the year.

Bruce Severns, Toorak

World.title: Discount fuel and cash giveaways: How Adrian Portelli’s business works
World.content:
NationalPetrol prices Discount fuel and cash giveaways: How Adrian Portelli’s business works Stephen Brook April 23, 2026 — 7:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Businessman Adrian Portelli was back in the news on Thursday after opening his new venture, selling fuel for $1 a litre at a petrol station in Preston. Also back in the news: questions about how the entrepreneur’s LMCT+ membership-based shopping discount and giveaway business actually works, and whether it is an unlicensed lottery, as critics and a South Australian regulator assert. Entrepreneur Adrian Portelli selling cheap fuel to his LMCT+ members at his petrol station in Preston today. Paul Jeffers On Thursday, the Preston petrol station was not ensnarled in the kind of traffic chaos that was seen at an earlier unrelated fuel giveaway in Truganina, organised by RS Rewards on Good Friday, which was shut down by police. But the cheap fuel is only available to members of LCMT+, who pay a monthly subscription fee to access hundreds of thousands of dollars’ worth of discounts, as well as cash and prize giveaways.



The new fuel membership will cost $99.99 a year, which gives members access to petrol at the wholesale price, Portelli told this masthead, adding that he launched the business after petrol companies declined to join his scheme. The Preston petrol station venture was not making money, he said. “We are not depending on this venture to turn a profit, it is a soft launch to test our [petrol station] employees,” he said. Over time, the number of petrol sites will expand. “We can’t lose money; otherwise, we will run out of money. ” LMCT+ is billed as a subscription platform that offers discounts to more than 2000 businesses. These include Ultratune, Elite Supplements, Rip Curl, home appliance shop Betta, Adore Beauty Interior Secrets and Frank & Beans Underwear. The business makes its money from subscriptions, as well as ticket sales for individual giveaways.



Until recently, there were three tiers of LMCT+ memberships. An entry-level membership, which goes for $19.99 a month, allows members to claim up to $50,000 in savings from affiliate businesses each year. With a premium membership ($49.99 a month), the annual savings cap increases to $150,000, and for the elite membership ($99.99 a month), it’s up to $250,000. The fuel membership, which costs $99.99 annually, will be available soon. Related Article Exclusive

Gambling Billionaire Adrian Portelli wants to sell you petrol as UK move raises gambling concerns Memberships also include a limited number of entries into LMCT’s famed giveaways, which became popularised thanks to Portelli’s appearances and purchases on The Block. On Thursday on ABC Radio, during an expletive-laden interview, Portelli denied he was cashing in on the fuel crisis or that his business was a gambling operation. “How is that gambling? We are using a trade promotion to promote the app,” Portelli, whose wealth has been estimated at $1.6 billion, told ABC Radio Melbourne.



Later that day he told this masthead: “When someone is choosing not to understand … That is the response you are going to get from me.” LMCT+, which stands for Licensed Motor Car Trader Plus, was founded by Portelli in 2018. The businessman became famous for buying up properties on home renovation program The Block, broadcast on Channel Nine (Nine owns this masthead), and offering them as giveaways on LMCT+. The program dubbed him “Lambo Guy” after a fondness for Lamborghini cars. Winner Brad (who requested a pseudonym as he didn’t want to be identified) received a winning call from Portelli telling him he had won either a house featured on The Block or $2.5 million. Related Article Petrol prices Free fuel hero or regulatory rebel? The chequered past of the man behind the Good Friday gridlock Brad, a business manager, was never an LMCT+ member but spent about $1200 over the previous year buying tickets for specific draws, also entitling him to shopping discounts, which he never used.



“If the person who won is not a member, they [members] tend to crack the shits,” said Brad, who added that he had missed watching the live draw on Facebook. “I was going to watch it and got into a conservation with my wife about something and my phone started ringing. I then jumped online and saw my name. “I didn’t believe it. In that moment, you are in shock.” Portelli called personally to announce the prize but at first “played coy” at the start by telling him he hadn’t won the lesser prizes before revealing he had the choice of $2.5 million or a house. Brad, who met Portelli by chance after his win, said he felt the businessman was the victim of the tall poppy syndrome. “You see the genuine excitement he gets; that’s what I take away from it.



“But I am going to have a different opinion to someone who hasn’t won,” he added, declining to reveal which prize he accepted. In South Australia, LMCT+ and Portelli are appealing against a ruling that found parent company Xclusive Tech Pty Ltd was guilty of conducting unlawful lotteries and fined it $40,000. Portelli was acquitted on personal charges and has threatened defamation action against the former South Australian gambling minister over her comments. “We run a legitimate business,” Portelli said. LMCT+ is running what it dubs the “the biggest giveaway in Australian television history” alongside Channel Seven and its new program My Reno Rules, after Portelli bought two homes in the Melbourne suburb of Bulleen that he intends to give away to the public on June 2.



The site has a live countdown to the giveaway draw, and any Australian resident over 18 can buy individual tickets to the prize draw, without subscribing. In the My Reno Rules giveaway, which promises winners the choice between one of the two houses or $2 million in cash, tickets go for as little as $10 for three entries, all the way up to $500 (1500 entries). The business says it is “fully licensed under Trade Promotion Lottery laws”, but gambling reform advocates are critical, saying the business operates through legal loopholes. Tim Costello, chief advocate for the Alliance for Gambling Reform, is a critic of Portelli and the gambling regulation system. “I think he has driven his Lamborghini through the loophole in gambling regulation,” Costello said. Costello said Australia operated in a “Swiss cheese patchwork of regulation” and national regulation was needed. He was also critical of the cheap petrol initiative.



“This is very clever. He will be seen by the public as the people’s hero. This is why he is a billionaire.” Earlier this month, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced a crackdown on “harmful and emerging online lottery products”, but did not name any specific businesses. “What is everywhere is innovative gambling,” Costello said. “You have prediction markets where you can bet on the Strait of Hormuz opening or closing. “There are so many offshore companies that are beyond any regulation. The online betting market is growing at 50 per cent a year.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Rinehart to hand over financial records to court rivals
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMining Rinehart to hand over financial records to court rivals Michael Philipps April 23, 2026 — 7:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

The decades-long legal battle that saw the descendants of iron ore pioneer Peter Wright claim victory against Gina Rinehart’s Hancock Prospecting will soon land in the hands of its fourth judge, as a row over the calculation of royalties brews. Rinehart is likely to be forced to hand over years of financial records to two rival mining dynasties. The WA Supreme Court judge who handed down the ruling in the case may not be available to oversee the ultimate decision of the royalties involved. Last week Justice Jennifer Smith ruled that Wright Prospecting was entitled to half of the historical royalties from the Hope Downs mines, estimated to be worth hundreds of millions of dollars. However, last year Smith was re-appointed as an Auxiliary Judge of the Supreme Court of Western Australia with her 12-month term beginning on June 5, 2025.



At the follow-up hearing to decide how the costs involved in the landmark case would be divided on Thursday, Smith said there will need to be some changes to the orders that the parties involved have proposed. “Having heard the parties this morning, there is a sufficient issue that has been raised that there are particulars of law that may not be able to be managed by a judge and should be handled by a referee,” she said. “Ultimately, both of these matters are appropriate to be defined by a referee and not an officer of a court “As I won’t be here much longer as a member of this court, I feel it is most appropriate that another judge make that decision.” Rinehart is likely to be forced to hand over years of financial records to two rival mining dynasties pursuing hundreds of millions of dollars in unpaid iron ore royalties.



Lawyers for Rinehart’s company, Hancock Prospecting, and the heirs of mining pioneer Peter Wright and engineer Don Rhodes wrangled over the implementation of a judgment that found Wright Prospecting and DFD Rhodes were owed some of the spoils from the massive Rio Tinto-operated Hope Downs mining complex, in WA’s ore-rich Pilbara region. These included who should calculate the royalty amounts, the interest rates that could be applied to the vast sum, potential damages for Hancock Prospecting’s breach of contract, future revenue payments and what documents Hancock Prospecting would be required to supply. In setting out her judgment last week, Smith called the decision only a “half-win” as she rejected Wright Prospecting’s claim for part ownership of another portion of the mining project, allowing Rinehart to keep her status as the country’s wealthiest person with an estimated fortune of $38 billion. Wright’s heirs, which include billionaire Angela Bennett and her nieces, Leonie Baldock and Alexandra Burt, argued that their family company was entitled to a 1.25 per cent royalty from the Hope Downs iron ore mines in WA’s Pilbara region. Hancock Prospecting runs the lucrative mines with mining giant Rio Tinto.



The tenements were first pegged by Hancock and Wright in the 1940s, and in 1982, the iron ore pioneers nutted out an agreement to divide the assets that was intended to prevent their descendants from arguing over ownership in the future. The parties will return to court on May 1 to continue the hearing. With AAP
